name: The Himley Hall Yews

location.address: Himley Hall and Park, Himley, Dudley DY3 (Staffordshire)

access: Free to walk in the park (Geograph caption, April 2026: free and open access between Himley Park and the adjoining Baggeridge Park; the hall itself is separately charged). Park owned by Dudley Council. Parking and event days may carry charges; check Dudley Council or Himley Hall.
transport: Himley is about 8 km south-west of Wolverhampton city centre, on the Dudley edge. A public transport route and journey time were not confirmed from a fetched page; treat as a bus-plus-walk day trip, not verified.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a cluster of about nine old yews among old oaks on the steep wooded slope above the hall. The largest is hollow, about 640 centimetres round; one tall, red-barked columnar yew stands among them.

photo.note: Not searched beyond AYG; AYG photos (Tim Hills 2003, Richard Roberts/Mike Glasson 2025) are copyright. Geograph SO8891 Himley Park photos exist (e.g. 8291494 by Roger D Kidd, CC BY-SA 2.0, taken 8 April 2026) but show the lake and park, not the yews; no yew photo viewed.

verify_notes: Ancient Yew Group (AYG) site record 'Himley Hall', site type parkland, access Public, owner Dudley Borough Council, grid ref SO88809160 (52.52216, -2.166498 converted OSGB36; site-level, not a tree fix). Recorded by Tim Hills 31 March 2003: nine yews mapped, 'there may be more'; approximate girths 21, 18, 17, 16, 14, 14, 11, 10, 10 ft. AYG database lists tree 1507 (638 cm at narrowest, 2-3 ft up, exactly 21 ft / 640 cm at 5 ft; more than half the circumference dead sapwood; roots spread a long way; 4 ft deep humus in the hollow), 1512 (564 cm close to ground; living wood round most of the bole), 1508 (518 cm at 60 cm, male, hollow, live wood on the path side), 1833 (488 cm at 150 cm), 1509 (488 cm), 1510 (442 cm). Tim Hills PDF 'The Yews of Himley Hall': tree 1 female, 14 ft 6 in at the ground, red-barked tall columnar, branches that overhung the house cut; tree 4 male, completely hollow above a large badger sett, about 16 ft, healthy foliage. History: a 1791 poem (Fitzgerald, 1801 Miscellaneous Poems) fixed on 'a very ancient yew of extraordinary size' on a hill near the mansion, standing among old oaks; Loudon 1838 'several immense yew trees, particularly one celebrated for its widely spreading head'; Garner 1844 yew 20 ft 10 in at 1 ft. 1791 poem and 1844 measurement match the present largest (about 21 ft) within measuring variation but identity of the 1791 tree with tree 1507 is not established; no age adopted. Drawing in the William Salt Library shows two lines of yews on the hillside above the moated manor. Alive: AYG tree pages carry photographs credited 2025 (Richard Roberts/Mike Glasson) and a site file dated 2025, so recent. Those 2025 notes on the AYG page are credited to the Woodland Trust Ancient Tree Inventory and were NOT used or cited here. Himley Hall: Wikipedia confirms Grade II* hall, park extended 1770s by Capability Brown, open to the public, owned by Dudley Metropolitan Borough Council. Park access: Geograph 8291494 (photo taken 8 April 2026) caption says free and open access between Himley and Baggeridge Parks. The yews are on a steep slope in the woodland, reached by paths; the exact trunk is not pinned. Group of nine folds into one collectible point only if the writer treats it as 'the yew slope'; best single tree is 1507. Single society database plus its historic citations plus ownership by a council; no independent modern measurement second source, so flagged.
story:
In 1791 a poet singled out "a very ancient yew of extraordinary size" on the hill beside Himley Hall, standing among old oaks. The hill still has yews among oaks. A survey in 2003 mapped nine of them and noted there may be more.

Whether today's largest is the poet's tree, nobody can prove. It measures about 640 centimetres round, 21 feet, and in 1844 a writer recorded a yew here at 20 feet 10 inches. That is close enough to tempt and not enough to settle it. In 1838 the garden writer Loudon described several immense yews at Himley, one celebrated for its widely spreading head.

The biggest is largely shell now. More than half its circumference is dead sapwood, and the hollow holds four feet of humus. The others have characters of their own. One female is tall, columnar and red-barked, the branches that once overhung the house since cut. A completely hollow male grows above a badger sett. Their girths step down from 21 feet to 10.

Capability Brown extended the park in the 1770s, and it now belongs to Dudley Council. Nobody has put an age on the yews, and we would rather say so than guess. Their records were updated in 2025.

The park is free to walk, on the Dudley edge about 8 kilometres south-west of Wolverhampton, with open paths through to Baggeridge Park; the hall charges separately. The yews are on the steep wooded slope above the hall.

name: Boningale Churchyard Yew

location.address: St Chad's churchyard, Boningale, near Albrighton, Shropshire WV7

access: Free. Open parish churchyard (AYG access: public); the yew is visible from the road.
transport: Shropshire village about 10 km west of Wolverhampton city centre (straight line from the coordinates).Albrighton station is on the Wolverhampton to Shrewsbury line; the walk from the station to Boningale and the journey time were not confirmed from a fetched page, so no minutes are claimed. Likely a train-plus-walk or car day trip.

location_site.name: St Chad's churchyard, south-east of the church

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the only yew in the churchyard, solid-looking from the road but hollow on its north side, with a horseshoe-shaped trunk. It stands south-east of St Chad's Norman church.

photo.note: AYG photos (Tim Hills 2012; Rev. Williams watercolour 1791, Shropshire Archives) are not open licence. Geograph/Commons church views exist (e.g. Geograph 1411813 'St Chad's, Boningale') but show the church; not checked for the yew.

verify_notes: Ancient Yew Group site record Boningale (nr Albrighton), St Chad, Lichfield diocese, churchyard, access public, owned by the Parochial Church Council, grid ref SJ81170259 (converted 52.620745, -2.279577; site level, not a tree fix), visited 7 April 2012 by Tim Hills. One yew, tree 3876, class 'V - con' (AYG veteran category), girth 396 cm at the ground; the 2019 site file says approximately 13 ft at the ground, male, viewed from the road it looks solid but the north side is hollow, horseshoe shape developing, considerable thickening on the eastern edge. It grows SE of a church that dates to Norman times (Wikipedia: built in the 12th century; Historic England lists the Church of St Chad, list entry 1053675, not re-read for the yew). The yew appears in Rev. Williams' 1791 watercolour held by Shropshire Archives (per AYG), so a yew of some size stood there in 1791; whether it is the same tree is by AYG's reading, not independently confirmed. No age estimate by AYG; age_min 230 is only the 1791 depiction (2026 minus 1791), not an age estimate. Alive: AYG photos from 2012 and a 2019 site file (the 2019 file text describes the tree as seen in 2012), so last confirmed 2012/2019; flagged. Single society record plus Historic England and Wikipedia for the church only. Modest girth. In Shropshire, outside Wolverhampton city; weaker candidate that fills the count.
story:
From the road, the Boningale yew looks solid. Walk round to its north side and it is hollow, the trunk opening into a horseshoe, with the wood thickening heavily along its eastern edge.

It is a male tree, 396 centimetres round at the ground, about 13 feet, when the Ancient Yew Group visited in 2012. That is modest beside the big churchyard yews of Tettenhall and Codsall, and it stands alone here, the only yew in the churchyard.

Its strongest evidence of age is a picture. A watercolour painted by the Reverend Williams in 1791, now held by Shropshire Archives, shows a yew at the church. The Ancient Yew Group reads it as this tree, which would make it more than 230 years old. Nobody has confirmed that the yew in the painting and the yew on the ground are the same, and nobody has put an estimate on its age, so the painting is a floor rather than a date. If you know more, tell us.

St Chad's is a Norman church, built in the 12th century, and the yew grows to its south-east. Our most recent first-hand description of the tree comes from that 2012 visit. We believe it still stands, and if you go, we would like to hear how it looks.

The churchyard is open and free, in a Shropshire village about 10 kilometres west of Wolverhampton. Albrighton, on the railway towards Shrewsbury, is the nearest station.

name: The Treebeard Oak, Sher Brook Valley

location.address: Brocton Coppice, Sher Brook Valley above the stepping stones, Cannock Chase, near Milford, Stafford ST17

access: Free. Open woodland on Cannock Chase; Brocton Coppice is a Site of Special Scientific Interest, so keep to the paths. The tree is off the main tracks, up a narrow path and a steep incline (Staffordshire Live, 12 Feb 2022). Staffordshire Live gives Punchbowl car park, just outside Milford, as the best place to park.
transport: Mostly reached by car; no public transport to the Chase edge was confirmed from a fetched page.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the oak that looks like Treebeard, with a hollow belly. It stands to the right of a narrow path after a steep climb, about five minutes from the Sher Brook stepping stones, off the main tracks.

photo.note: Staffordshire Live photos are copyright. No open-licence photo found; a Geograph search was blocked (Cloudflare challenge).

verify_notes: Staffordshire Live (Samuel Hodgkiss, 12 Feb 2022): an oak in Sher Brook Valley, Brocton Coppice, 'five minutes walk from the stepping stones', that 'looks rather much like Treebeard'; the article's photo caption mentions 'inside the belly of the tree' (a hollow); Barry Collis, chairman of Chase Ramblers, quoted that it is not common and off the beaten track somewhat; article says trees in Brocton Coppice date back two or three centuries, some to the time of Henry VIII (a coppice-wide statement, not about this tree). Directions in the article: from the Punchbowl car park by Milford, walk down to the stepping stones, turn right up the next main path, then right up a narrow path for about 100 yards, bear right where it splits, continue up a steep incline veering slightly left, and the tree is on the right. PIN: no coordinate for the tree itself was found. The pin given is the OSM node 2687569925 'Stepping Stones' (52.77791, -2.02014, ford=stepping_stones, seen in an OSM map download); the tree is some hundred metres from that, so the pin is a reference point, not the tree. A Komoot highlight 5877116 'Ancient Tree in Cannock Chase' sits at 52.771897, -2.020145 (about 650 m south of the stepping stones; tip by Paul, 3 July 2023: 'absolutely beautiful ancient tree that must be at least 500 years old'); it is NOT confirmed to be the same tree as the Treebeard oak (more than five minutes' walk), so it was not adopted. No age adopted: the 500 years is a walker's remark. Alive: article dated 12 Feb 2022 describes it standing; no later dated photo seen for the same tree (Komoot 2023 tip is of uncertain identity), so flagged. Species 'oak' per the article only. Single news source for the tree (the second and third URLs are for the stepping-stones pin and the Coppice setting only); weaker than cnk_002. Do not mix up with the Groot Tree (cnk_002, about 400 m west at 52.77713, -2.02471).
story:
Brocton Coppice has two oaks named after trees that walk in films. One is the Groot Tree. This is the other, said to look like Treebeard from The Lord of the Rings, and it hides further from the main tracks. When Staffordshire Live wrote it up in February 2022, the chairman of a local ramblers' group called it off the beaten track.

The paper's directions are the best map there is. From the Punchbowl car park just outside Milford, walk down to the stepping stones over the Sher Brook and turn right up the next main path. After about 100 yards, turn right onto a narrow path, bear right where it splits, and climb a steep slope veering slightly left. The oak is on your right, about five minutes from the stones. Our pin sits on the stepping stones, not the tree, because nobody has published a position for the trunk itself.

The article's pictures show its hollow belly. Nobody has dated it. The same article says trees in Brocton Coppice go back two or three centuries, some to the time of Henry VIII, but that is a statement about the wood, not this trunk. Even the species is unconfirmed beyond oak, so if you can tell sessile from pedunculate, tell us which.

The last dated account we have is that 2022 article. Brocton Coppice is a Site of Special Scientific Interest, free and open, so keep to the paths on the way in.
